title: REQUESTS
description:
Requests is an open-source Python HTTP client library for making human-friendly HTTP/1.1 requests to web services and APIs. It provides simple convenience functions and APIs for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS, and custom HTTP methods, with support for URL parameters, form-encoded and JSON payloads, multipart file uploads, streaming request and response bodies, chunked transfer encoding, and configurable character encodings.

Its core objects include `Request`, `PreparedRequest`, `Session`, `Response`, and `HTTPAdapter`. Sessions manage persistent settings, cookies, authentication, headers, proxies, TLS verification, client certificates, connection pools, environment configuration, redirects, response history, and transport connections. Prepared requests support detailed request construction and validation, including URL preparation, parameter merging, authentication, content-length calculation, body rewinding, hooks, and case-insensitive headers. The built-in HTTP adapter performs blocking network I/O and manages HTTP and HTTPS connections, proxies—including SOCKS proxies—timeouts, streaming, retries, TLS behavior, certificate verification, and connection pooling.

Requests supports Basic, proxy, Digest, OAuth, and custom authentication mechanisms, including credential encoding and digest-header generation. It handles redirects, authentication stripping, cookies through `RequestsCookieJar`, response hooks, proxy selection and bypass rules, URL parsing and requoting, header and content-type parsing, and environment-based settings. Responses expose status codes and aliases, headers, cookies, raw and decoded content, text, JSON parsing, link-header information, streaming iteration, encoding detection, connection cleanup, and HTTP error validation.

The library defines structured exceptions for request failures, connection errors, invalid URLs and headers, timeouts, excessive redirects, HTTP errors, retries, decoding failures, chunked encoding problems, SSL failures, and warnings. It also provides status-code mappings through `codes`, case-insensitive and lookup dictionary structures, compatibility helpers, cookie utilities, certificate handling, and diagnostic information about installed SSL and IDNA components.

Requests relies on related packages such as urllib3 for low-level HTTP handling and connection management, Certifi for trusted CA certificates, IDNA for internationalized domains, and Charset Normalizer or legacy Chardet support for encoding detection. Its compatibility layer exposes selected networking dependencies and utilities under `requests.packages`, while modules provide URL joining, string and Unicode helpers, file-length calculation, JSON and content-encoding detection, and other internal networking functions.

The project is hosted on GitHub, documented at `requests.readthedocs.io`, distributed through PyPI, and uses the Apache-2.0 license. The referenced project version is 2.32.3, with source code under `src/requests`; its tests extensively cover request construction, sessions, adapters, authentication, cookies, redirects, streaming, uploads, headers, proxies, TLS, response processing, exceptions, and HTTP behavior.

title: GITHUB
description:
GitHub is a web-based software development, code-hosting, and API platform that hosts the Requests project and related repositories, including requests-oauthlib, Kerberos and NTLM authentication support, urllib3, and pytest-httpbin. It provides the source repository tarball, project and repository URLs, download and dependency statistics, issue trackers, and references to numerous Requests issues, including issues 2018, 2356, 3772, and 482, as well as GH #3579.

GitHub’s APIs are used throughout the Requests documentation and tests to demonstrate HTTP functionality. Examples include retrieving repository commits, events, issues, and issue comments; creating, editing, and deleting comments; inspecting supported HTTP methods; and sending JSON-encoded POST and PATCH requests through the GitHub API v3. GitHub’s REST API also demonstrates pagination metadata exposed through HTTP `Link` headers.

The `github.com` and `api.github.com` hostnames appear in tests and examples covering URL-prefix matching and ordering for `HTTPAdapter`, user-agent headers, HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects, properly configured HTTPS certificates, API endpoint behavior, and server metadata. GitHub therefore serves both as a real-world external service referenced by the Requests project and as a representative host for testing HTTP requests, redirects, authentication-related integrations, URL handling, API interactions, and response headers.

title: KENNETH REITZ
description:
Kenneth Reitz is a software developer and the author and copyright holder of the Requests Python HTTP library, with project materials crediting him and associating him with the library’s 2012 documentation. He is identified in GitHub data as both the author and committer of commit `A050FAF`, and as the GitHub user `kennethreitz`, whose comment and repository API links appear in example test responses.

Kenneth Reitz is also associated with the `kennethreitz.org` website and domain, which are used in Requests documentation and tests as examples for building HTTPS requests and demonstrating disabled SSL verification. The domain appears in a Requests request-building test and in an example HTTPS request. His email-style identifier, `me@kennethreitz.com`, is used as the authentication realm in a test server’s digest-authentication challenge. Together, these references connect Kenneth Reitz’s personal website, GitHub identity, and authorship of the Requests project.

title: URLLIB3
description:
urllib3 is a Python HTTP and networking library used by Requests as its underlying transport implementation. It provides HTTP and HTTPS connection handling, connection pooling and TCP connection reuse, persistent connections, proxy support and proxy managers, request transmission, URL parsing, TLS and SSL configuration, timeout management, retry handling through its `Retry` class, and networking-related exceptions.

Requests imports urllib3 directly and exposes it through `requests.packages.urllib3` while preserving module identity. It uses urllib3 for standard and proxy-enabled HTTP adapters, connection-pool creation, proxy authorization, transport configuration, response processing, and streamed response handling. When available, urllib3’s `HTTPResponse` and raw response streams supply response data for iteration and cookie extraction. Requests also relies on urllib3 utilities such as `make_headers`, `parse_url`, request fields, multipart form-data encoding, and HTTP-related request handling that expects bodies supporting the bytes-like interface.

urllib3 defines the timeout behavior represented by Requests’ `Urllib3Timeout` compatibility layer and supplies exceptions related to HTTP errors, protocol failures, decoding, timeouts, and SSL operations. Requests wraps or reuses these exceptions, including using urllib3’s `HTTPError` as the base for `ContentDecodingError`. Its connection objects, certificate settings, pool keys, and TLS configuration are also used by Requests when establishing and managing connections.

urllib3 is a runtime dependency of Requests, supported in versions 1.21.1 or newer but below version 3. Requests checks its installed version for compatibility and may enable fallback behavior. urllib3 version differences affect compatibility: the 1.x series provides `SNIMissingWarning`, while urllib3 2.0 removed that warning and changed related behavior by raising an error instead. Its version is also included in Requests’ diagnostic and bug-report information.

title: HTTPBIN
description:
HTTPBIN (also known as httpbin or httpbin.org) is an HTTP request and response testing service used extensively in the Requests documentation, examples, and test suite. It serves as the base URL and fixture for generated test endpoints over both HTTP and HTTPS, allowing Requests behavior to be exercised against predictable endpoints that inspect, echo, delay, redirect, or otherwise manipulate HTTP traffic.

The service supports tests and demonstrations involving standard and custom request methods, including GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS; URL query parameters; form-encoded data; multipart form submissions and file uploads; request bodies; headers; cookies; user-agent inspection; and response serialization. It also provides endpoints for setting and retrieving cookies, returning submitted request data, generating streamed responses, compressed or gzip responses, HTML and malformed response headers, delayed responses, specific status codes, and redirects, including POST redirects and configurable redirect targets.

HTTPBIN is additionally used for authentication examples and integration tests, including Basic Authentication and Digest Authentication. It acts as the destination for demonstrations of response hooks, secure HTTPS requests, header handling, request and response behavior, and general authenticated HTTP usage. In streaming examples, httpbin.org provides the source of streamed HTTP responses.

The related `httpbin` Python package is a dependency, approximately version 0.10.0, that provides HTTP request and response testing utilities and supports the fixture-based testing environment.

title: WIKIPEDIA

title: REQUEST
description: REQUEST is a user-created object in the Python Requests library that represents an HTTP request before it is prepared or transmitted. It is constructed from an HTTP method—such as GET—and a target URL, along with optional headers, files, form data, JSON payloads, query parameters, authentication, cookies, and hooks. The Request object defines the request’s content and behavior, can be prepared into a PreparedRequest, and may then be sent to a server directly or through a session.

title: RESPONSE
description: The `RESPONSE` entity is the `Response` Python class in the Requests library, representing the HTTP result returned by a server after a request or prepared request is sent. It contains the originating request and response metadata, including the status code, URL, headers, cookies, encoding, body content, raw response, connection, and elapsed time. The `Response` object supports content access and decoding, iteration over response data, streaming, serialization, and context-manager behavior. It is also used during redirect handling to inspect response status codes and provides mechanisms for evaluating status behavior and raising errors for unsuccessful HTTP responses.

title: PREPAREDREQUEST
description:
PREPAREDREQUEST is a Requests library object that represents a fully prepared HTTP request ready for transmission through a connection to a server. It is created from a `Request` or `Session` after Requests processes the HTTP method, URL, query parameters, headers, authentication, cookies, files, form data, JSON payload, body, and hooks. The object stores the exact request data that will be sent, including its final URL, headers, cookies, and body, while retaining request encoding and hook functionality.

Although prepared for transmission, PREPAREDREQUEST remains mutable and can be modified before it is sent. It is associated with the resulting `Response`, may represent the next request in a redirect chain, and supports serialization and restoration through pickle testing.

title: REQUESTS API
description: The Requests API is a public interface for sending HTTP requests and provides helper methods including `delete`, `get`, `head`, `options`, `patch`, `post`, `put`, and `request`. It also offers `requests.get` for making direct HTTP requests and `requests.Session` for creating persistent sessions, enabling users to reuse configuration and connections across multiple requests.

title: OPENSSL
description: OPENSSL is a cryptographic software project and library that provides SSL/TLS functionality. Its version information may be collected directly or through PyOpenSSL, which exposes OpenSSL capabilities to applications. OpenSSL also supplies the `c_rehash` utility, used to process certificate directories for SSL certificate verification by Requests. It serves as the underlying SSL technology supporting modern secure connections, including PyOpenSSL-related HTTPS behavior.

title: SESSION
description: SESSION is a Requests library client object that manages persistent state and configuration while sending multiple HTTP and HTTPS requests. It stores and applies cookies, headers, authentication, proxy settings, hooks, environment settings, certificates, and TLS verification options. SESSION creates and mounts HTTPAdapter instances to contact HTTP and HTTPS URLs, maintaining separate connection pools when TLS configurations differ and providing connection pooling for efficient reuse. It prepares and sends requests, including prepared requests, resolves redirect chains subject to configured redirect limits, and manages the adapters used for network communication. SESSION also supports pickling and serves as the central mechanism for maintaining consistent request behavior across a series of HTTP operations.

title: HTTP
description: HTTP is both the application-layer network protocol used for communication between clients, servers, local response servers, and the httpbin testing service, and a Python standard-library package that supplies cookie- and HTTP-related compatibility imports. It is used to validate status codes, response headers, content lengths, and response bodies, and it underlies documented `Request`, `Session`, and `PreparedRequest` operations. Requests exercises HTTP through standard methods including GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, and OPTIONS, as well as custom verbs. HTTP support also includes transport adapters, configurable request handling, proxy usage, and standard response processing.

title: HTTPS
description: HTTPS is the secure form of HTTP used to protect web communications through TLS encryption. It is supported by Requests for secure connections, including connections to local TLS test servers, and can be configured through transport adapters, SSL settings, and proxy configuration. HTTPS relies on SSL/TLS certificate verification and trusted certificate authorities to authenticate servers and help ensure that communications are established with the intended endpoint.

title: SSL
description: SSL is the security and networking technology provided in Python through the standard-library `ssl` module. It enables secure client-server communication by establishing TLS-encrypted connections, verifying HTTPS certificates, and handling TLS certificates through objects such as `SSLContext`. Python applications can use SSL to create client-authentication contexts and wrap HTTP server sockets with TLS. Requests conditionally imports and uses SSL to determine native Server Name Indication (SNI) support, establish secure HTTPS connections, and validate certificates; certificate-verification failures are exposed through Requests’ `SSLError` exception. The module also provides access to system OpenSSL version information. Tests may check SSL for modern `SSLContext` availability and related TLS functionality.

title: TLS
description: TLS is the secure transport security protocol used by the local HTTP server through Python’s SSL context. It protects communications by supporting certificate verification, trusted certificate bundles, connection-pool separation, and mutual TLS configurations. Disabling certificate verification weakens TLS security by allowing untrusted certificates, increasing exposure to man-in-the-middle attacks.

title: HTTPADAPTER
description: HTTPADAPTER is the built-in Requests transport adapter for HTTP and HTTPS URLs. It is mounted on URL prefixes, typically through a Requests session, to deliver requests through the underlying urllib3 transport layer. HTTPADAPTER creates and manages connection pools and urllib3 connections, supports proxy managers, applies TLS and SSL certificate verification settings, and provides standard request-related connection methods. It also manages serialization state and adapter-specific cleanup. As the default adapter for HTTP and HTTPS, HTTPADAPTER can be configured with retry behavior, including retry-enabled handling for HTTPS requests, and can be extended for custom SSL or other connection settings.

title: BASEADAPTER
description: BASEADAPTER, also known as `BaseAdapter`, is an abstract transport adapter class used by the Requests library. It defines the fundamental operations required for transport adapters, including certificate verification and closing connections. The class is intended to be subclassed when implementing custom Requests transport adapters. Because it provides an interface rather than a complete implementation, some of its methods may raise `NotImplementedError` until they are overridden by a concrete subclass.

It controls the number of retry attempts for failures such as DNS lookup errors, socket connection failures, and connection timeouts. RETRY also defines backoff behavior, status-based retry conditions, and the HTTP methods eligible for retrying.

title: PYTHON
description:
Python is the programming language and runtime ecosystem in which the Requests library, its compatibility layers, authentication tests, cookie-handling code, HTTP request preparation, socket server, and related asynchronous projects are developed and used. The code supports multiple Python implementation variants and addresses compatibility between Python 2 and Python 3, particularly for strings, bytes, iterators, generators, exceptions, JSON serialization, file-like objects, and standard UTF-8 decoding.

Python provides the runtime features and standard-library modules used throughout the codebase, including `datetime`, `encodings`, `io`, JSON support, `hashlib`, `os`, `re`, `urlparse`, and class methods. It also supplies the underlying mechanisms for HTTP functionality, request preparation, authentication, cookie compatibility, and network communication. The `requests.compat` module specifically manages version-dependent behavior and portability across supported Python environments.

title: PYTEST
description:
Pytest is the Python testing framework used to define, organize, and execute the Requests project’s test suite. It supports test functions and classes, parameterized and parametrized test cases, assertions about results, HTTP response status codes, Requests data structures, and request behavior, as well as checks for expected failures.

Pytest provides fixtures for reusable test setup, including temporary directories, URL preparation, local server configuration, and environment-variable manipulation through the `monkeypatch` fixture. The suite uses exception assertions such as `pytest.raises` to verify expected failures, including SSL errors, `CookieConflictError`, JSON-decoding errors, invalid request-sending errors, and other Requests-specific exceptions.

The framework also supports conditional skips, test markers, warning checks, and failure handling. Within the Requests project, Pytest is invoked by the custom test command to run the suite. Its configuration enables doctest execution with specified doctest options, requires Pytest version 6.2 or newer, and directs test discovery to the `tests` directory.

Requests requires IDNA versions 2 or later but earlier than version 4, with the dependency constraint specifically indicating version 2.5 or newer and below 4. The package reports its installed version through a module attribute, and Requests’ help functionality optionally inspects that information. Tests also cover environments where the version attribute is missing and cases where IDNA reports version 2.6.

title: COOKIEJAR
description: COOKIEJAR is a generic Python HTTP cookie-management class from `http.cookiejar` that serves as a standard cookie container for Requests, including `RequestsCookieJar` and compatible implementations. It stores and manages cookies, applies cookie policies to HTTP requests and responses, and can be attached to Requests sessions to retain outstanding cookies. CookieJar supports iteration, cookie removal, policy management, and adding cookies from dictionaries. It can be copied generically by creating a shallow copy, clearing the copied jar, and inserting copies of the original cookies.

title: REQUESTSCOOKIEJAR
description: RequestsCookieJar is the default cookie-container implementation used by Requests sessions to store, persist, merge, set, retrieve, remove, and inspect cookies associated with HTTP requests and responses. It extends Python’s `http.cookiejar.CookieJar` while implementing a dictionary-like `MutableMapping` interface, allowing dictionary-style `__getitem__`, `__setitem__`, and `__delitem__` operations as well as compatibility with dictionary-based cookie insertion and updates. RequestsCookieJar supports copying while preserving both its cookie policy and contents, and it can be serialized with pickle by excluding its unpickleable `_cookies_lock` from the serialized state and restoring the lock afterward. For cookie lookup, it uses `_find_no_duplicates` when strict retrieval is required and `_find` when it may arbitrarily choose among cookies with conflicting names. It therefore combines standard cookie-jar behavior with convenient mapping semantics for managing cookies throughout Requests sessions.

title: INTERNAL_UTILS

It provides utilities for validating HTTP headers and includes the `to_native_string` compatibility helper, which normalizes HTTP header values into native string representations.

title: COMPAT

The module also provides compatibility aliases and imports such as `Morsel`, `MutableMapping`, `cookielib`, `urlparse`, and `urlunparse`. In addition, COMPAT includes helpers for proxy handling, URL processing, string and mapping operations, integer utilities, and quoting usernames and passwords for safe inclusion in URLs.

title: READY EVENT
description: The ready event signals that the server socket has been created and bound, allowing callers entering the server context to continue.

title: STOP EVENT
description: The stop event signals that the server thread has completed and the server socket has been closed.

title: WAIT TO CLOSE EVENT
description: The optional wait-to-close event allows the server to remain open until an external signal is received, with a five-second timeout.
